title: One and ones
subtitle: I've already got one / his early ones
summary: Use one and ones in place of a countable noun, and know when they must be left out and when they must stay.

lesson.heading: Instead of repeating a noun
lesson.text: We use one instead of repeating a singular countable noun, and ones instead of repeating a plural noun, when the context makes clear what we are talking about.

examples.text: *A:* Can I get you a drink? *B:* It's okay, I've already got **one**.
I think his best poems are his early **ones**.

lesson.heading: Not with uncountables, not without a defined group
lesson.text: We never use one / ones for an uncountable noun, and we can't use ones unless we say precisely which group of things we mean. Where the group is not defined, use some.

examples.text: If you need any more paper, I'll bring you **some**.
I asked him to get apple juice, but he got **orange**.
*A:* We need new curtains. *B:* Okay, let's buy **some**.

lesson.note: Ones is fine as soon as the group is defined: let's buy green ones this time / ... ones with flowers on / ... those ones.

lesson.heading: Nouns used as adjectives, and possessives
lesson.text: We don't use one / ones after a noun that is working as an adjective. After possessive determiners (my, your, her) we prefer mine, yours, hers, although possessive + one / ones is often heard in informal speech.

examples.text: I thought my memory stick was in my trouser pocket, but it was in my **coat pocket**.
I'd really like a smartphone like **yours**.
examples.note: '... like your one' is heard in informal speech

lesson.heading: Things rather than people
lesson.text: We usually keep ones for things. It is more likely with people in comparative sentences, and in a few fixed phrases.

examples.text: We need two people to help. We could ask **those men** over there.
Older students seem to work harder than younger **ones**.
the little **ones** (= small children), (your) loved **ones** (= usually close family), (one of) the lucky **ones**

lesson.heading: Where one / ones can be left out
rows: When we buy medicines, we have no way of knowing which (**ones**) contain sugar.
Look at that pumpkin! It's the biggest (**one**) I've seen this year.
The last test I did was quite easy, but some parts of this (**one**) are really difficult.
either, neither, another, each, the first / second / last
Karl pointed to the paintings and said I could take either (**one**). She cleared away the cups, washed each (**one**) thoroughly, and put them on the shelf.
lesson.note: Some people think 'those / these ones' is incorrect, particularly in formal English.

lesson.heading: Where one / ones must stay
lesson.text: We don't leave out one / ones after the, the only, the main and every, or after an adjective.

examples.text: When you cook clams you shouldn't eat **the ones** that have broken shells.
After I got the glasses home, I found that **every one** was broken.
My shoes were so uncomfortable that I had to go out today and buy some new **ones**.

lesson.note: After a colour adjective we can often leave one out in answers: 'Have you decided which jumper to buy?' 'Yes, I think I'll take the blue (one).'

lesson.text: Ask two questions before writing ones: is the noun countable, and have I said which group I mean? If the answer to either is no, use some.

exercises.prompt: Bilal brought in the wood and put ___ on the fire.
exercises.explanation: Wood is uncountable, so one / ones is impossible - use some.

exercises.prompt: Normally I don't like wearing a scarf, but it was so cold I put ___ on.
exercises.explanation: One stands for a singular countable noun (a scarf).

exercises.prompt: *A:* We've run out of potatoes. *B:* I'll get ___ when I go to the shops.
exercises.explanation: No particular group of potatoes is defined here, so we use some, not ones.

exercises.statement: We haven't got lemon tea, but you could have mint one instead.
exercises.explanation: ... but you could have mint instead. / ... you could have some mint instead. Tea is uncountable, so one is not possible.

exercises.statement: *A:* What kind of cakes do you like best? *B:* Ones with cream inside.
exercises.explanation: Correct. 'With cream inside' defines exactly which group we mean, so ones is fine.

exercises.prompt: I couldn't fit all the boxes in the car, so I had to leave ___ behind and pick it up later.
exercises.explanation: 'Pick it up' shows that only one box was left behind, so the singular one is right.

exercises.prompt: I answered most of the questions, but had to miss out some very difficult ___.
exercises.explanation: After an adjective we keep ones; here it replaces the plural noun questions.

exercises.statement: There are lots of gloves here. Are these your ones?
exercises.explanation: Are these yours? After a possessive we prefer mine, yours, hers, though 'your ones' is heard informally.

exercises.prompt: Most of the trees in our garden are less than ten years old but ___ are much older than that.
exercises.explanation: Ones can't be used without defining the group, so we use some.

exercises.prompt: Make a comparison about how hard students of different ages work.
exercises.answer: Older students seem to work harder than younger ones.
exercises.explanation: Ones refers to people mainly in comparative sentences like this one.

exercises.prompt: Could the repeated noun in each sentence be replaced by one or ones?

items.text: I answered most of the questions, but had to miss out some very difficult questions.
The issue discussed at the meeting was an extremely complicated issue.
Diana takes photos of old buildings. There's an excellent photo of a local church in her office.
He used to work for a finance company, but he's moved to an insurance company.
*A:* Are you picking Jo up at the train station? *B:* No, she's arriving at the bus station.
On one channel was a war film and on the other was a horror film.

exercises.prompt: Can one or ones be left out of each sentence?

items.text: I like both of these jackets. I don't know which one to choose.
The books were so disorganised that I soon lost track of which ones I had already counted.
Each winter seemed to be colder than the last one.
Can you remember where you bought this one?
The vases are all handmade and every one looks different.
There are many excellent food markets in town but the main one is near the port.
I drove around the houses, looking for the ones with 'For Sale' notices outside.
